excerpt: Workers' compensation is a legally required insurance programme, not an optional perk. What Georgia and South Carolina employers must provide.
keyTakeaways: Workers compensation is a legally mandated insurance program — not an optional employee benefit — that provides medical care and wage replacement for work-related injuries. Georgia requires coverage for employers with 3+ employees (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-1 et seq.), while South Carolina requires it for 4+ employees (S.C. Code § 42-1-10 et seq.). Benefits include TTD, TPD, PPD, medical treatment, vocational rehabilitation, and death benefits. Filing deadlines are 1 year in Georgia and 2 years in South Carolina.

faqs.question: Is workers compensation a benefit or a legal right?
faqs.answer: Workers compensation is a legally mandated insurance program, not a voluntary employee benefit. Both Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-1 et seq.) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 42-1-10 et seq.) require qualifying employers to carry coverage. Unlike optional benefits like health insurance, workers comp is automatic and cannot be opted out of.

faqs.question: Which employers are required to carry workers compensation in Georgia and South Carolina?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, employers with 3 or more employees must carry workers compensation insurance. In South Carolina, the threshold is 4 or more employees. Both full-time and part-time workers count toward these thresholds.

faqs.question: What benefits does workers compensation provide?
faqs.answer: Workers compensation provides medical benefits covering all authorized treatment, temporary total and partial disability benefits (typically two-thirds of average weekly wages), permanent partial and total disability benefits, vocational rehabilitation, and death benefits for surviving dependents.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a workers compensation claim?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, you must report the injury within 30 days and file a formal claim within 1 year (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82). In South Carolina, you must report within 90 days and file within 2 years (S.C. Code § 42-15-40). Missing these deadlines can jeopardize your benefits.

faqs.question: Are independent contractors covered by workers compensation?
faqs.answer: Generally, independent contractors are not covered by workers compensation. However, if you are misclassified as an independent contractor but actually function as an employee (set schedule, employer-provided tools, direct supervision), you may still qualify for benefits.

faqs.question: Can my employer fire me for filing a workers compensation claim?
faqs.answer: Both Georgia and South Carolina prohibit employer retaliation for filing a legitimate workers compensation claim. If you believe you were terminated or demoted because you filed a claim, an attorney can help you pursue legal remedies in addition to your workers comp benefits.
